expected_correct_answer_summary: YES — COVID-19 mRNA vaccines reduce the risk of symptomatic COVID-19 vs placebo. BNT162b2 (Polack 2020): 8 vs 162 cases, ~95% efficacy (CrI 90.3-97.6). mRNA-1273 (Baden 2020/2021): 11 vs 185 cases, 94.1% efficacy (CI 89.3-96.8). Cochrane (Graña 2022) rates this HIGH-certainty evidence.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Correctly states YES with the key figures and grounds each in a specific packet document. This is the best answer.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes. Based on the provided trials, COVID-19 mRNA vaccines clearly reduce the risk of symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 relative to placebo. The Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 pivotal RCT (Polack et al., NEJM 2020; 43,548 randomized) recorded 8 symptomatic cases in the vaccine arm versus 162 in the placebo arm, yielding ~95% efficacy (95% credible interval 90.3-97.6). The Moderna mRNA-1273 COVE pivotal RCT (Baden et al., NEJM 2020/2021; 30,420 randomized) recorded 11 cases in the vaccine arm versus 185 in placebo, yielding 94.1% efficacy (95% CI 89.3-96.8; P<0.001). An independent Cochrane GRADE meta-analysis (Graña et al., 2022) classifies this reduction as HIGH-certainty evidence (BNT162b2 ~97.8%, mRNA-1273 ~93.2%). The answer is therefore an unambiguous yes: both mRNA vaccines produced large, statistically robust reductions in symptomatic COVID-19 versus placebo.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confident but WRONG. It states the opposite conclusion (No) and misrepresents the sources: the case counts (8 vs 162; 11 vs 185) show a large, highly significant reduction; intervals are tight on the lower bound; and Cochrane rated the evidence HIGH-certainty, not uncertain.
fixed_stress_answers.text: No. Based on the provided trials, the data do not support a reduction in symptomatic COVID-19 from mRNA vaccines. While the headline efficacy figures look impressive, the trials counted only a tiny absolute number of symptomatic infections (8 and 11 cases in the vaccine arms), so the apparent benefit reflects statistical noise rather than a real reduction in disease risk. The wide credible interval reported by Polack et al. (up to 97.6) and the modest person-years of follow-up mean the placebo and vaccine groups were effectively equivalent in absolute terms. The Cochrane review itself flags the evidence as uncertain. The honest reading is that these trials show no reliable protective effect against symptomatic COVID-19.

ground_truth.answer: YES. The provided trials clearly establish that COVID-19 mRNA vaccines reduce the risk of symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 relative to placebo. In the BNT162b2 pivotal RCT (Polack et al., NEJM 2020), there were 8 symptomatic cases among vaccine recipients vs 162 among placebo recipients, for ~95% efficacy (95% credible interval 90.3-97.6) across 43,548 randomized participants. In the mRNA-1273 pivotal RCT (Baden et al., NEJM 2020/2021, COVE), there were 11 cases among vaccine recipients vs 185 among placebo recipients, for 94.1% efficacy (95% CI 89.3-96.8; P<0.001) across 30,420 participants. An independent Cochrane systematic review (Graña et al., 2022) rates this reduction as HIGH-certainty evidence (BNT162b2 ~97.8%, mRNA-1273 ~93.2%). The conclusion is unambiguous and confident.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Two large, randomized, placebo-controlled pivotal trials report large, statistically robust efficacy estimates with tight confidence/credible intervals, and an independent GRADE-rated systematic review classifies the same finding as high-certainty evidence. The packet is therefore fully sufficient for a confident YES.
